title: Westcreek Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Westcreek wells have a 250 ft median depth, 6.0 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $22,200-$37,000.
h1: Westcreek Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Westcreek sits in Douglas County mountain terrain where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured bedrock. The local record includes 491 wells within five miles, though only 316 are recorded as constructed. That distinction matters: permit records show the local pattern, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce on a particular lot.

For planning purposes, the typical Westcreek well is about 250 feet deep and reports a 6.0 gpm median yield. A finished well costs more than drilling alone, and site access, trenching, electrical work, storage, and the pump can materially affect the bid.

sections.heading: How deep are Westcreek wells?
sections.html:
Westcreek wells have a median reported depth of 250 feet. The middle half runs from 130 to 380 feet, so a driller estimating a new well here should not rely on the median alone. Most recorded wells fall between 100 and 300 feet, while another substantial group reaches 300 to 600 feet.

The local range is wide. 14% are under 100 feet, 44% are 100 to 300 feet, 36% are 300 to 600 feet, and 6% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,250 feet. Granite and gneiss can change quickly from one lot to the next, so nearby completed wells are useful for bidding but are not a guarantee.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Westcreek well make?
sections.html:
The reported median well yield near Westcreek is 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 2.3 and 9.8 gpm. That is a workable range for many household systems, but the pumping rate is only one part of the evaluation. Storage capacity, recovery, pressure equipment, and the intended household use also matter.

Low-producing wells are present in the records: 7% report under 1 gpm, while 34% report 1 to 5 gpm. Most, at 57%, report 5 to 15 gpm, and 2% exceed 15 gpm. Ask for the well construction report and yield test before treating a neighboring result as an expectation for your lot.

sections.heading: Westcreek water levels and the local trend
sections.html:
Among the 26 wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 99 feet. The middle half is 61 to 159 feet below the surface. This is the water level when the well is not being pumped, not the same thing as the depth of the well or the water available during sustained pumping.

The decade figures suggest a possible change that deserves investigation: the median reported static level was 68 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 125 feet in the 2020s. The sample is limited, and measurement conditions may differ, so this does not prove a basin-wide decline. For a purchase, compare recent well tests, pump settings, and neighboring records rather than relying on the median alone.

sections.heading: Westcreek permit history and local drillers
sections.html:
Westcreek has a long permit history, with the largest recorded decade totals in the 1990s and 1980s. The records show 108 permits in the 1990s, 87 in the 1980s, and 80 in the 1970s. Permits continued into the present, with 27 in the 2020s and the newest permit year listed as 2025.

The most active names in these records are Woods Drilling Inc. (Woods, William D.) with 68 permits, Mountain Well Improvement LLC (Wiley, David D.) with 66, and Woods Drilling Inc. (Woods, William L.) with 63. These are permit-record counts, not endorsements. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost near Westcreek?
sections.html:
Westcreek drilling is priced around fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The supplied cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 250 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $16,200 to $25,000.

A finished system is estimated at $22,200 to $37,000 when the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work are included. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed quote. Depth, difficult rock, access for the rig, casing and grout requirements, power distance, and site layout can move the total. Get the drilling and completion scope in writing, including what happens if the hole is low-yield or dry.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 474 wells use that description. Only 4 identify an alluvial aquifer, and none are listed in a Denver Basin aquifer. Fractured bedrock can produce good water on one parcel and poor water on another, making low yield, a dry hole, and variable recovery important risks to price and investigate.

There are 26 historic mine features and 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site mapped within about 10 miles. No EPA Superfund or cleanup sites are mapped in that area. That does not replace water testing. Test an existing well for relevant contaminants, inspect casing and grout, locate the septic system and replacement area, and confirm the lot can meet well, septic, driveway, and building requirements.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Westcreek lot
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit, construction report, pump test, and service history for any existing well. Verify the actual static level, tested yield, pump depth, storage, and water quality. If the lot is vacant, review nearby records from Westcreek and surrounding mountain communities such as Woodland Park, Perry Park, Palmer Lake, Divide, Florissant, and Larkspur, while giving the greatest weight to wells closest to the parcel.

Before closing, have a driller discuss likely depth, access, casing and grout, and the cost of a low-yield outcome. Confirm the intended permit and household use with DWR. Exempt household-use wells have a 35 gpm pumping limit, and over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan. Coordinate the well location with septic, the home, electrical service, and winter access before construction begins.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Westcreek, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth for wells within five miles of Westcreek is 250 feet. The middle half runs from 130 to 380 feet. Records range widely: 14% are under 100 feet, 44% are 100 to 300 feet, 36% are 300 to 600 feet, and 6% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,250 feet.

faq.q: What is the typical well yield in Westcreek?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 6.0 gpm, with the middle half between 2.3 and 9.8 gpm. About 7% of wells report under 1 gpm, while 34% report 1 to 5 gpm. Most, 57%, report 5 to 15 gpm. A nearby well helps with planning, but fractured bedrock results can vary sharply between lots.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Westcreek?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 250-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $16,200 to $25,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $22,200 to $37,000. Access, depth, rock conditions, and low-yield work can change the bid.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Westcreek?
faq.a: Well safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The records show 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 26 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped there. Test an existing or new well for appropriate contaminants, and inspect the wellhead, casing, grout, and septic separation.

faq.q: Are Westcreek well water levels going down?
faq.a: Only 26 wells report static water levels, so the trend is limited. The median depth to water was 68 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 125 feet in the 2020s. That suggests a possible decline, but different measurement conditions may affect the comparison. Review recent neighboring tests and the subject well's own records before drawing a conclusion.
